papers.title_in_file: FraudTransformer: Time-Aware GPT for Transaction Fraud Detection
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)
papers.what_it_is: A GPT-style sequence model with time and positional encoders, tested on an HSBC payment fraud dataset against logistic regression, XGBoost and LightGBM.

assertions.value: The authors report that, on a large industrial dataset, FraudTransformer surpasses the classical baselines and the transformer ablations, and delivers the highest AUROC and PRAUC on the held-out test set.
quotes: Experiments on a large industrial dataset—tens of millions of transactions and auxiliary events—show that FraudTransformer surpasses four strong classical baselines
On the held-out test set it delivers the highest AUROC and PRAUC.
assertions.certainty_reason: One study on one proprietary dataset, three runs, with an undersampled test set.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract says four baselines but lists three, and the conclusion says three; the count is inconsistent inside the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evaluation data were sampled to conceal the fraud rate, that the test fraud rate is around 43 percent through undersampling non-fraud cases, and that results may differ at other fraud rates.
quotes: The evaluation dataset was sampled to conceal the fraud rate of the main data.
this rate does not represent the fraud rate in the whole dataset but is instead obtained through undersampling non-fraud cases
with a 43% fraud rate in our evaluation set, the random baseline is 0.43
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup and scope.
assertions.reader_inference: Absolute PRAUC values here are not comparable with PRAUC on a realistic fraud rate; only relative differences are meaningful.

assertions.value: The authors state that training and evaluation are deterministic with fixed splits, so the standard deviation of the baseline results is zero.
quotes: All runs used fixed train/validation/test splits and deterministic hyperparameters
the standard deviation of the results for the three baselines are zero
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own setup.

papers.title_in_file: Inductive inference of gradient-boosted decision trees on graphs for insurance fraud detection
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)
papers.what_it_is: A graph gradient boosting machine (G-GBM) for heterogeneous graphs, tested on insurance fraud data.

assertions.value: The authors report that G-GBM performs on par or better than the state of the art on an open-source and a real-world proprietary insurance fraud dataset.
quotes: We demonstrate G-GBM for insurance fraud detection on an open-source and a real-world, proprietary dataset, and find that G-GBM performs on par or better than the state-of-the-art.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from two datasets in one study.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the HCP dataset the gain from neighbourhood information is less pronounced, and the AUC-PR is slightly larger for LightGBM than for G-GBM.
quotes: The HCP dataset shows a setting in which the gains from graph-based neighbourhood information are less pronounced.
The AUC-PR on the other hand is slightly larger for LightGBM than for G-GBM.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one dataset.

assertions.value: The authors state that one downside of the method is the expansion of dimensions, which can become computationally impractical in highly connected graphs, many node or edge types, or high-dimensional features.
quotes: One downside of our method is the expansion of dimensions, which can become computationally impractical in the case of highly connected graphs, many node/edge types, high-dimensional features, or any combination thereof.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own limits.

papers.title_in_file: Conformal Inference for Open-Set and Imbalanced Classification
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)
papers.what_it_is: A conformal prediction method (conformal Good-Turing) for classification with unseen labels and extreme class imbalance.

assertions.value: The authors report that on simulated and real data their method gives prediction sets with valid coverage in open-set scenarios with infinitely many possible labels, and more informative predictions under extreme class imbalance.
quotes: we demonstrate our method leads to prediction sets with valid coverage even in challenging open-set scenarios with infinite numbers of possible labels, and produces more informative predictions under extreme class imbalance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on simulated and real data in one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that selective sample splitting breaks exchangeability but finite-sample guarantees are kept through re-weighting.
quotes: Despite breaking exchangeability, this allows maintaining finite-sample guarantees through suitable re-weighting.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own theoretical claim; the reader did not check the proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that the method tends to be more conservative than standard conformal prediction in closed-set settings, and that no upper bound on coverage is guaranteed.
quotes: no corresponding upper bound is guaranteed
our method tends to be more conservative than standard conformal prediction in closed-set settings
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own limits.

papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)
papers.what_it_is: A theory and algorithm (MILD) for two-stage learning to defer when a few experts dominate (expert imbalance).

assertions.value: The authors report that MILD shows clear improvements over existing baselines on image classification and on real-world LLM routing tasks.
quotes: Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing clear improvements over existing baselines on both image classification and real-world Large Language Model (LLM) routing tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the imbalance they address concerns experts, not class labels, so standard class-imbalance techniques do not apply directly.
quotes: the imbalance we aim to correct concerns experts, not class labels
This distinction between labels and experts complicates the direct application of traditional imbalancehandling techniques.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope.
assertions.reader_inference: This paper is not about rare-class fraud labels; its imbalance is over which expert is favored, so it bears on fraud only indirectly.

assertions.value: The authors report that with synthetic experts MILD consistently achieves lower deferral loss than TDEF, and with real experts consistently outperforms TDEF across all settings.
quotes: MILD consistently achieves lower deferral loss by allocating experts closer to the optimal distribution.
MILD consistently outperforms TDEF across all settings.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study.

papers.title_in_file: High Performance, Low Reliability: Uncertainty Benchmarking for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)
papers.what_it_is: A benchmark of tabular foundation models, gradient-boosted trees and baselines on 112 datasets, using conformal prediction coverage.

assertions.value: The authors report a performance-uncertainty trade-off: tabular foundation models achieve the highest AUC but show lower conditional coverage (SSCS) than GBDTs on the 112 TALENT datasets.
quotes: although TFMs achieve the highest predictive performance (AUC), they exhibit lower conditional coverage under conformal prediction (SSCS) compared to GBDTs
comparing TFMs, GBDTs, and classical baselines on the 112 datasets of the TALENT benchmark
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one benchmark study.

assertions.value: The authors report that on 20 synthetic datasets with high noise and weak class separation foundation models reach the highest AUC but have lower SSCS than GBDTs.
quotes: Foundation models achieve the highest AUC, but their SSC remains comparatively low
we generate 20 synthetic datasets with high noise and weak class separation
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from synthetic data in one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the analysis is limited to small and medium-scale datasets and to a model-agnostic conformal framework.
quotes: Our analysis is limited to small and medium-scale datasets and to a modelagnostic conformal framework.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own limits.

papers.title_in_file: Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)

assertions.value: The authors introduce an open source suite of application-oriented benchmarks that map the fidelity of results as a function of circuit width and depth, using volumetric benchmarking.
quotes: we introduce an open source suite of quantum application-oriented performance benchmarks
framework of volumetric benchmarking
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own method.

assertions.value: The authors state that the tested hardware suggests substantial advances are required for quantum computers to outperform their classical counterparts on useful tasks.
quotes: The performance of the hardware that we tested suggests that substantial advances are required for quantum computers to outperform their classical counterparts on useful tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' interpretation of results from selected cloud devices.

assertions.value: The authors state that some benchmarks need exponentially expensive classical computation and are infeasible for O(100) qubits, and that their execution time measurement is rudimentary.
quotes: they will be infeasible for O(100) qubits
our measurements of execution time are currently rudimentary
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own limits.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Volume in Practice: What Users Can Expect From NISQ Devices
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)
papers.what_it_is: Independent quantum volume measurements on 24 NISQ devices from five vendors.

assertions.value: The authors report that quantum volume values achieved in their tests typically lag officially reported results and depend significantly on the classical compilation effort invested.
quotes: QV values achieved in our tests typically lag behind officially reported results and also depend significantly on the classical compilation effort invested.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study of 24 devices at one time.

assertions.value: The authors report the highest QV they measured per vendor: IBM 16 with default transpilation and 32 with more optimized compilation, Quantinuum (lower bound) 512, IonQ 8, Rigetti 8.
quotes: The highest QV values we measured for each vendor are IBM at 16 using default transpilation and 32 when using more optimized compilation, Quantinuum (lower bound) at 512, IonQ at 8, Rigetti at 8
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from a 2022 snapshot; device results change over time.

assertions.value: The authors state that passing a QV test often relies on selecting a good qubit subset, which compromises the intuitive appeal of the QV measure.
quotes: even if a device passes a QV test, such success often relies on selecting a good qubit subset, which is not trivial to identify
This fact slightly compromises the original intuitive appeal of the QV measure
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' interpretation of their results.

papers.title_in_file: Benchmarking simulated and physical quantum processing units using quantum and hybrid algorithms
papers.partial_detail: abstract, introduction, method, results, conclusion (key sections)
papers.what_it_is: A runtime, cost and fidelity benchmark of simulators and four physical QPUs using quantum neural networks, by the company that runs one of the tested services.

assertions.value: The authors report that the QMware cloud service reduces runtime by up to 78 percent compared with the next fastest option for algorithms with fewer than 27 qubits.
quotes: Results show the QMware cloud computing service can reduce the runtime for executing a quantum circuit by up to 78% compared to the next fastest option for algorithms with fewer than 27 qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors are from Terra Quantum and QMware, the company whose service is reported as fastest.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors' affiliation is the tested vendor, so the runtime ranking is a vendor self-measurement.

assertions.value: The authors report that of the four quantum devices tested, only IonQ's Harmony achieves high fidelity with more than four qubits, and that the high financial cost of physical QPUs is a barrier.
quotes: only IonQ’s Harmony achieves high ﬁdelity with more than four qubits
the high ﬁnancial cost of physical quantum processing units presents a serious barrier to practical use
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study in 2022.

assertions.value: The authors state that the investigation is not an exhaustive benchmark of all available systems.
quotes: This investigation is not an exhaustive benchmark
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own scope.
